newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian shares break barrier, take aim at record.
newsitem.headline: Indian shares break barrier, take aim at record.

text.p: Indian shares hit a 33-month high on Wednesday, jumping over two percent on a surge in foreign investment, and analysts expect the benchmark index to soon break into record territory.
"The market has gone into a new orbit," said P.C. Mohnot, assistant general manager, market operations, at the Unit Trust of India (UTI), the country's largest mutual fund.
"There should be no apprehensions of a fall. The market will get past record highs," he told Reuters.
The benchmark 30-share Bombay Stock Exchange (BSE) index leapt 98.30 points, or 2.28 percent, to end Wednesday at 4,404.69 -- piercing 4,400 for the first time since mid-October 1994.
"It has crossed the barrier. The market looks in very good shape," said Ketan Jhaveri, chief dealer at Kotak Securities, the Indian affiliate of Goldman Sachs.
Analysts expect the market to beat its record high of 4,643.31 set on September 12, 1994, propelled mostly by foreign funds and the prospect of stronger corporate earnings this year.
"Compared to other emerging markets, India is doing very well," said UTI's Mohnot. "Improved perception and liquidity is driving this market."
Traders said foreign institutional investors (FIIs), armed with fresh profits from booming U.S. markets, were the chief buyers on Wednesday.
"There's been frenzied buying by FIIs," said Sanat Dalal, a top broker at the BSE. "They are accumulating all the blue-chips."
Other dealers said foreign funds were currently enlarging their portfolios by buying into new sectors.
"The FIIs are strengthening their portfolio by adding multinational shares to other blue-chips," said Arun Shah, chief dealer at brokerage P.R. Subramanyan & Sons.
Indian shares have also been supported by expectations for improved corporate results for fiscal 1997/98 (April-March), the analysts said.

"Corporate India seems to be signalling a better year in FY1998 (financial year ending March 31, 1998) based on our analysis of the results of nearly 250 companies," Pravin Shah at Morgan Stanley Dean Witter said in a report.
He said about one-fourth of Indian companies raised dividends for 1996/97 despite lower earnings.
"We believe that these higher dividend payouts reflect managements' optimism for the current year and beyond," he said.
Traders said the buoyant market lured more investors while sellers were becoming more selective.
"The biggest point to note is that the most prominent seller has stopped selling," said Dalal, referring to the Unit Trust of India.
